note: Bluesky posts for the agentwright-cron worker (workers/cron/bsky.mjs). Each item is posted once at or after `at` (within 3 hours; later it is skipped and reported). Max 300 graphemes. Optional `link`: shown as a link card. The card is built by fetching the page from the worker, so use `link` only for our own pages: a site behind bot protection (Product Hunt answers 403) gives a card with nothing but the URL. Put such a URL at the end of `text` instead; it becomes a clickable link. First week: 1-2 posts/day, at most 1 link post/day. Optional `reply_to` (the at:// URI of a post, taken from `node scripts/bsky-replies.mjs`): the item is posted as a reply; the worker refuses it unless that post is a reply to us, a mention of us or a quote of us, and a reply must not go out 03:00-07:00 KST. No automated follows, likes, reposts or DMs, and never a reply to someone who did not write to us first. Longer questions are steered to our blog comments. The worker runs at :07 every hour, so the real posting time is the first :07 at or after `at`. A linked blog post must already be open (its date, KST) when the item goes out, or the link is a 404 with an empty card. Edit on main; no redeploy needed. Before merging a change to this file run `npm run check:queues` (real posting times, length limits, links to posts that are not open yet). Top-level "paused": true stops all posting.

posts.text:
Agentwright Starter is on Product Hunt today: a Next.js starter kit for Claude-powered agent SaaS with per-user cost tracking.

If you build on the Claude API, we'd like to hear what a kit like this is still missing.

https://www.producthunt.com/posts/agentwright-starter

If your Claude agent's prompt cache hit rate drops for no clear reason, check the order of your tools.

Tool definitions sit at the front of the cached prefix. Load MCP servers in a different order and every request pays full input price again.

In a typical Claude Sonnet 5.5 request (4,000 tokens in, 600 out, 60% cached), output is 13% of the tokens and 64% of the cost.

If you want a smaller bill, look at max_tokens and answer length before you trim the prompt.

A $20/month AI plan on Claude Sonnet 5.5, 300 requests per user: 76% margin.

The same user at 10x usage: -52%. Break-even is about 1,900 requests a month.

Worked numbers and a free calculator for your own inputs. Questions go in the comments on the post; we answer there.

Same request on Claude Sonnet 5.5, 4,000 tokens in and 600 out:

0% cache hits: $0.0140
60% cache hits: $0.0094

One cache_control line on the system prompt. Check it before you touch your pricing.

Agentwright Starter: a Next.js 16 codebase for Claude agent SaaS with the agent loop, per-user cost metering, plan caps, auth and billing already wired.

$99 for the first 50 licenses (list $149), one-time, lifetime updates, 14-day refund.

Read the code first: https://agentwright.app/inside/

A SaaS boilerplate gives you sign-in, payments and a landing page.

A product where an agent does the work needs more, because every request costs you money: a tool loop with a turn limit, a usage row per model call, plan caps checked before the call, and evals in CI.

Haiku, Sonnet or Opus? Pick the model per route (chat, summaries, background jobs), not per message.

Cost per request at current prices, sensible effort defaults, and the API differences that bite when you switch. Questions go in the comments on the post; we answer there.

The last line of defence most AI apps forget: a monthly spend limit on the API provider's side.

It is the only limit that still works when your own metering code has a bug.

A 2M-token monthly cap can cost you $0.20 (all cache reads on Sonnet) or $40 (all output on Opus).

Cap each user's spend in dollars, and reserve the worst case before the request so two parallel calls can't slip past. Code on our blog.

Schema-valid JSON from Claude in TypeScript: output_config.format with messages.parse(), when strict tools fit better, which JSON Schema features are supported, and the three cases where you still have to check the result. Questions go in the comments on the post; we answer there.

Not every Claude call has a user waiting: nightly digests, tagging, evals, backfills.

Send those through the Message Batches API and they cost half the standard price. Most batches finish within an hour; requests not done in 24 hours expire.

Claude Haiku 5.5 bills a prompt over 100,000 tokens at long-prompt prices, and it does so for the whole request.

99,000 tokens in, 1,000 out: $0.0104
101,000 tokens in, 1,000 out: $0.053

2% more context, 5x the cost. If a retrieval step can overshoot, cap it below the line.

Six SQL queries over a per-request usage table: who costs the most, who costs more than they pay, which model drives the bill, whether caching works, and whether today looks abnormal. Questions go in the comments on the post; we answer there.

A 200 from the Claude API is not always a finished answer.

end_turn, tool_use, max_tokens, stop_sequence, pause_turn, refusal: what a production agent loop should do with each, including truncated tool calls. Questions go in the comments on the post; we answer there.

Storing Claude agent conversations: keep every content block (tool calls, tool results, thinking) and append only.

Editing earlier turns breaks prompt caching and can return 400s on current models. What to do instead when history gets long:

Retrying a Claude call inside an agent loop is easy. Not re-running the tool that already charged a card is the hard part.

429, 500, 529, dropped streams: what the TypeScript SDK retries for you and what you must handle yourself.

We made a free remote MCP server for Claude API pricing.

Add https://agentwright.app/mcp to Claude Code, Claude Desktop or Cursor and ask "what does this workload cost on Sonnet vs Haiku?" It knows caching and Batch API prices.

No sign-up, no key.

Claude's token counting endpoint is free and takes the same input as a real request.

Worth the extra round trip for uploads, budgets and routing. For a chat turn, the previous response's usage is often the better estimate. Questions go in the comments on the post; we answer there.

Long-running Claude agent conversations: clear old tool results with context editing, or let the server compact at a token threshold.

How each interacts with prompt caching and billing, and the one mistake that silently turns compaction off.

What a Next.js boilerplate for a Claude agent SaaS has to cover beyond login and payments: the tool loop, token and cost metering per user, price snapshots, plan caps, prompt caching, billing webhooks, MCP tools and evals.

One table, with a post that has the code for each part.

Starting from a free chat template? Before you charge for the product, you add four things: billing webhooks that set each user's plan, a usage row per model call, caps that belong to a plan, and evals.

Vercel's free Chatbot template next to our paid kit, and when the free one is the better start.

Human approval for agent tool calls: classify tools, stop the Claude loop on a gated call, store the pending action, show the exact arguments, execute once, and resume with the right tool_result. Questions go in the comments on the post; we answer there.
Row-level security as a second lock behind WHERE user_id = ...: policies, a non-owner app role, set_config per transaction, agent tools in the same scope, connection poolers, and what to test.

Fast, free tests for a Claude agent: tools as plain functions, input schema tests, and a scripted fake client for the loop. The checks that need the real model stay in a separate eval suite. Questions go in the comments on the post; we answer there.
The architecture of a Claude agent SaaS, following one request: auth, rate limits, spend limits, model choice, the tool loop, streaming, metering and storage, with a detailed post for each step.

A Stop button for a Claude agent with AbortController: cancel the stream and the tools, keep the conversation valid, and still record the tokens you paid for when a stream ends early. Questions go in the comments on the post; we answer there.

Catch a runaway AI bill before the invoice: a daily total against a budget, a per-user spike against that user's own history, an hourly burn-rate check, and the provider-side limit as the last safety net.

Onboarding emails for an AI SaaS, triggered by what users did: welcome, first success, 80% of the plan, limit reached, a quiet check-in. A Postgres jobs table, idempotency keys and one-click unsubscribe. Questions go in the comments on the post; we answer there.

A document search tool for a Claude agent on plain Postgres: a generated tsvector column, a GIN index, websearch_to_tsquery for model-written queries, ranked short results, and the signs it is time to add vectors.

Trace every Claude agent run in two Postgres tables: runs and steps, with timings, tokens, stop reasons, errors and the API request id. Then p95 latency and failing tools are one query each. Questions go in the comments on the post; we answer there.
Half-price Claude calls for work nobody waits for: which jobs fit the Message Batches API, a table to track them, a cron job that submits and collects by custom_id, and per-user metering.

Hybrid keyword and vector search for an agent's tool in one Postgres query: pgvector next to the tsvector, an HNSW index, reciprocal rank fusion, and a small test set to prove it helped. Questions go in the comments on the post; we answer there.
PDF uploads in a Claude agent: base64 or the Files API, the limits for your upload form, the token cost before you send, file ids scoped per user, and deleting files when users delete their data.

One click, one agent run: a client-generated idempotency key, a unique constraint in Postgres, and a reattach path that replays the stored answer instead of paying for a second run. Questions go in the comments on the post; we answer there.
Web search for a Claude agent: the server tool, max_uses and domain filters, citations, pause_turn, sending encrypted results back unchanged, and metering the $10 per 1,000 searches per user.

Most agent bugs that look like model mistakes are tool definition mistakes. Names, descriptions that say when to call a tool, strict schemas, useful results and error messages, with before/after examples. Questions go in the comments on the post; we answer there.

Export my data, delete my account: one written map of where user data lives in an AI product (Postgres, files at Anthropic, email and payment providers, logs), an export job, a deletion job, and a test.

Kill switches for an AI agent: turn off a tool, change a model, lower limits or pause one user in seconds, without a deploy. A config table, a short cache, an audit log and a runbook. Questions go in the comments on the post; we answer there.
